phenomenon.name: Belphegor
phenomenon.subcategory: Demon of sloth / prince of Hell

description.summary: A demon in Christian demonology, derived from the Moabite god Baal-Peor of the Hebrew Bible. In Peter Binsfeld's 1589 classification he is the prince of sloth, and one of the seven princes of Hell.
description.full: Belphegor is a major demon in Christian demonology, derived from the Hebrew Bible's Baal-Peor (בַּעַל פְּעוֹר), a Moabite deity worshipped on Mount Peor in Numbers 25:1–5 and condemned in Hosea 9:10 and Psalm 106:28. The English form Belphegor reaches us through Latin Belphegor / Beelphegor and entered demonological literature through medieval and early-modern grimoires. Peter Binsfeld's Tractatus de confessionibus maleficorum et sagarum (1589) names Belphegor the chief demon of sloth (acedia) in the seven-deadly-sins / seven-princes-of-Hell schema. In the slightly earlier Lanterne of Light (a 15th-century English Lollard text), he is paired with gluttony rather than sloth. Jacques Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire infernal (1818, illustrated 1863) calls him Hell's ambassador to France, makes Mary Magdalene his enemy, and depicts him as a horned, bearded male figure or, in a separate tradition, as a woman. Niccolò Machiavelli's novella The Story of Belfagor the Archdevil (Belfagor arcidiavolo, c. 1518–1527) sends Belphegor to Earth to investigate marriage; Pierre de Larivey adapted the story in 1607. The 1965 French novel and 1965 ORTF television series Belphégor, le fantôme du Louvre revived the figure in modern popular culture.

etymology.origin: From Hebrew Baʿal-Pəʿôr (בַּעַל-פְּעוֹר), 'Lord of Peor' — Peor being a place in Moab where this deity was worshipped (Num 25). Latinized in late antiquity and the Middle Ages as Belphegor.
etymology.meaning: Literally 'Lord of (the place) Peor'. Some demonological writers (including the modern Wikipedia gloss) translate Pəʿôr as 'gap', yielding 'Lord of the Gap', but this gloss is not universally accepted in biblical scholarship.
etymology.first_use: 13th century BCE setting in the Hebrew Bible (Num 25); demon-name in Latin Christian sources from the early modern period; foregrounded in Peter Binsfeld's 1589 demon classification

taxonomy.subtype: Prince of Hell / demon of sloth

related_phenomena.description: Other major demon-prince derived from a biblical foreign deity (Philistine Baʿal Zəvuv)

related_phenomena.name: Belial
related_phenomena.description: Other major demon-prince in Jewish-Christian tradition

related_phenomena.name: Asmodeus
related_phenomena.description: Demon assigned to lust in Binsfeld's seven-princes schema

related_phenomena.name: Lucifer
related_phenomena.description: Demon assigned to pride in the Binsfeld schema

features.description: Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire infernal (illustrated edition, 1863) depicts Belphegor as a horned, bearded man enthroned on a chamberpot — a satirical motif tied to his cult
Some traditions depict Belphegor as a beautiful woman, the form he is said to take when he appears to humans

physical.morphology: No fixed canonical form. Iconography divides between the horned demon-king of Collin de Plancy and a female form found in older demonological lore.

abilities.description: In Binsfeld's classification, Belphegor's specific role is to tempt humans into laziness, apathy and acedia
Some demonological writers say he tempts humans by suggesting wealth-bringing inventions
In some early-modern sources he reveals secrets and helps make discoveries

patterns: Tempts through ease, wealth, and laziness
Cited as Hell's ambassador to France in 19th-century demonology

range.description: Originating in the Moabite cult of Baal-Peor in the Hebrew Bible. Developed as a named demon in medieval and early modern Christian demonology, especially in Latin, French, and Italian sources.
countries: Worldwide in Christian and esoteric demonology

hotspots.name: Mount Peor (Moab)

location.description: Mount Peor in ancient Moab, east of the Jordan River

hotspots.notes: Cult site of Baal-Peor mentioned in Numbers 25; etymological origin of Belphegor

peak_activity_periods.description: Christian demonological systematization (Binsfeld 1589) and Machiavelli's Belfagor arcidiavolo
Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire infernal (1818, ill. 1863) standardizes the iconography
Belphégor as Phantom of the Louvre in Arthur Bernède's 1927 novel and the 1965 ORTF television series

origins.cultural_roots: Moabite religion (Baal-Peor) reinterpreted by Hebrew tradition as a foreign idol and (in later Christian readings) as a demon.
origins.earliest_accounts: Hebrew Bible, Numbers 25:1–5 (incident at Shittim where Israelites worship Baal-Peor) and parallels in Hosea and Psalms.
origins.folklore_connections: Part of the medieval Christian conversion of foreign biblical gods into demons (Beelzebub, Belphegor, Dagon, Astaroth).

timeline.event: Niccolò Machiavelli writes Belfagor arcidiavolo (publ. posth. 1549), a comic novella in which Belphegor is sent to Earth to investigate human marriage
timeline.significance: First major literary treatment of Belphegor

timeline.event: Peter Binsfeld classifies Belphegor as the demon of sloth in the seven-princes-of-Hell schema
timeline.source: Binsfeld, Tractatus de confessionibus maleficorum et sagarum (1589)

timeline.event: Jacques Collin de Plancy publishes Dictionnaire infernal, with Belphegor as Hell's ambassador to France
Illustrated edition of Dictionnaire infernal includes the famous horned-Belphegor woodcut by Louis Le Breton
Arthur Bernède's novel Belphégor, le fantôme du Louvre
timeline.significance: 20th-century repositioning of the figure as a popular phantom

timeline.event: Belphégor, le fantôme du Louvre television series airs on ORTF (France); a 2001 film remake follows
timeline.significance: Cements Belphegor in modern French popular culture

history.modern_era: Belphegor is best known today through Collin de Plancy's iconography, Machiavelli's novella, the Belphégor of the Louvre tradition, and as a recurring figure in fantasy and horror media. He is also referenced in popular economics as 'the Belphegor prime' (1000000000000066600000000000001), so named because of its embedded sequence of digits.

documentary.name: Numbers 25:1–5
documentary.description: Account of Israelites at Shittim worshipping Baal-Peor; etymological origin of Belphegor.
documentary.analysis: The biblical incident at Shittim provides the demon's name and theological backdrop.

documentary.name: Peter Binsfeld, Tractatus de confessionibus maleficorum et sagarum (1589)
documentary.description: Demonological treatise classifying Belphegor as the prince of sloth in the seven-princes-of-Hell schema.
documentary.analysis: Standard reference for the deadly-sin / demon mapping repeated across early modern demonologies.

documentary.name: Jacques Collin de Plancy, Dictionnaire infernal
documentary.description: Major 19th-century compendium of demons; entry on Belphegor with the Le Breton woodcut.
documentary.analysis: Source of the most widely reproduced modern image of Belphegor.

paranormal.name: Demon of sloth
paranormal.description: Belphegor is a real spiritual being who tempts humans to acedia / sloth, one of the seven princes of Hell.

scientific.name: Demonization of a Moabite deity
scientific.description: Modern biblical scholarship treats Belphegor as a Christian demonization of the Moabite deity Baal-Peor, following the standard pattern of converting rival biblical gods into demons.

skeptical.name: Literary and theological construct
skeptical.description: Belphegor is a literary and demonological construct without empirical referent; a useful figure for moral, narrative, and esoteric purposes rather than a phenomenon to be investigated.
evidence_cited: Continuous reinvention from Numbers 25 to Machiavelli to modern pop culture

traditions: French popular tradition (Belphégor of the Louvre)
stories: Machiavelli's Belfagor sent to Earth to test marriage
folklore.beliefs: In Christian demonology, Belphegor presides over sloth; in French popular tradition, he is a romantic phantom of Paris; in early-modern Italian comedy, a fish-out-of-water archdevil unable to survive marriage.

other: Le Breton illustration (1863) widely reproduced in occult and pop culture

research.ongoing_studies: Belphegor is studied within biblical reception history, the history of Christian demonology, and the literary history of the Renaissance comic devil tradition.
